paper_title: Innata-0: A Native Embodied World System with Model-Agent Co-Design

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: The physical world is open-ended, dynamic, and partially observable. While foundation models have advanced embodied intelligence, standalone models struggle with long-horizon execution, and simply integrating models with agents may lead to inconsistencies between planning and physical control. To support reliable and adaptive behaviors in the physical world, we introduce Innata-0, a native embodied world system. Innata-0 jointly designs an embodied world-action model and an agent to combine their complementary strengths. The model, Innata-0-WAM, adopts a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that integrates understanding, prediction, and action generation. The agent, Innata-0-Agent, coordinates long-horizon execution through memory, verification, and recovery. A co-design protocol is further proposed to align model training with agent execution and leverage validated experiences to support subsequent adaptation and model improvement. Extensive evaluations demonstrate strong embodied capabilities across understanding, world prediction, and robotic manipulation. Innata-0 represents our first step toward physical intelligence, and we see it as the beginning of a much longer journey.

Native Model-Agent Co-Design The physical world is open-ended, partially observable, and dynamically evolving, where actions have uncertain consequences and failures may incur irreversible costs. While foundation models have substantially advanced embodied intelligence, standalone foundation models still struggle to sustain reliable behavior over long horizons, particularly when execution requires self-correction and adaptation. Extending their capability boundaries therefore requires coupling native model capabilities with persistent agentic reasoning [1, 2], memory [3, 4], and interaction [57]. However, simply integrating models and agents may not fully realize their combined potential. Inconsistencies between planning and control may lead to unreliable physical execution and limited adaptation from accumulated experience. This motivates shift from standalone embodied model toward native embodied world system. To this end, we characterize native through three core capabilities: Plan lays the foundation for the system to accomplish long-horizon tasks by coordinating model execution across subtasks; Recover further bolsters the system, enabling it to handle uncertainties and recover from unexpected failures during real-world execution; and Evolve extends the system to continuously adapt to new environments and scenarios through accumulated experience. To jointly realize these capabilities, we introduce Innata-0, model-agent co-designed system that advances native embodied intelligence. As illustrated in Figure 1, our co-design establishes complementary roles for the embodied model and agent, allowing the model to fully leverage its native capabilities while the agent extends its effective operating scope. On the model side, Innata-0-WAM serves as the physical execution foundation of the system. We adopt tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture [8], which provides understanding, prediction, and action generation capabilities. The model is conditioned on the complete instruction, active subtask, and verified task history. By incorporating currentand history-plan annotations during training, Innata-0-WAM aligns its learned conditioning interface with the agents evolving representation of task progress. On the agent side, Innata-0-Agent serves as the system coordinator, supporting long-horizon planning, failure recovery, and continual evolution. It orchestrates model execution across subtasks while maintaining hierarchical memory. Grounded in observations and execution feedback, the agent verifies against intended physical outcomes and invokes tool-based recovery upon deviations. Verified interactions and experiences are consolidated into reusable skills that refine subsequent decisions and recovery strategies. Innata-0-Agent aligns its execution logic with the models capabilities, enabling coordinated execution, outcome verification, and experience-driven adaptation. Realizing Plan, Recover, and Evolve requires the model and agent to work together and play complementary roles. We therefore establish co-design protocol that enables them to operate in concert, leveraging their respective strengths while guiding their subsequent design. Crucially, this protocol operates in both directions: the models execution capabilities shape how the agent organizes and delegates tasks, while the agents requirements for planning, recovery, and adaptation guide model design and training. Our protocol aligns the models training data with the agents task instructions, subtask plans, and recovery commands, allowing complex tasks to be carried out through coordinated execution. The agent, in turn, validates execution outcomes and consolidates experiences to refine its task commands and reusable recovery strategies. It also feeds successful rollout segments, including corrective actions and post-recovery continuations, into the shared data pipeline for subsequent policy training. These principles guide our data construction, model training, and agent design, laying the foundation of native embodied intelligence. We evaluate the physical capabilities underlying Innata-0 and their use in closed-loop task execution. Among the compared models, the understanding tower ranks first on nine benchmarks and within the top two on fourteen. On WorldArena 2.0 Track 1 [9], Innata-0 achieves an EWM score of 67.63, the highest among the open-source models. Policy evaluations on RoboCasa365 [10] and RoboDojo-Sim [11] examine manipulation and task completion. On RoboCasa365, Innata-0 achieves 60.2% overall success and ranks first on AtomicSeen tasks with an 88.4% success rate. These evaluations characterize the models grounding, prediction, Innata-0 Technical Report and control capabilities, as well as its use within an agent-guided execution loop. To conclude, we propose Innata-0, native embodied world system that extends physical intelligence beyond individual task execution. Our approach jointly designs the embodied model and agent to leverage their complementary strengths. shared interaction protocol aligns model capabilities with agent requirements and guides data construction, model training, and agent design. Together, these designs enable long-horizon planning, failure recovery, and continual evolution. Our system co-design establishes basis for studying how aligned task context, physical-outcome verification, and validated experience contribute to reliable open-world interaction. 2. Embodied Data Construction 2.1. Overview Raw visual, linguistic, action, and tactile data contain rich knowledge about objects, interactions, and physical processes, yet their existing annotations make only part of this knowledge explicit. Following the co-design protocol, we make task goals, subtask relationships, and completion evidence explicit, while preserving the links between corrective behavior and subsequent task execution. We therefore develop Task-Oriented Knowledge Refinement, unified data construction pipeline that extracts shared annotations from heterogeneous sources and prepares supervision tailored to each learning objective and training stage. Each source can support multiple training tasks wherever the necessary observations and annotations are available. The resulting task annotations align the models training context with the agents subtask objectives for Plan. Corrective trajectories and task continuations provide supervision for Recover, while validated rollout segments enter the same pipeline for subsequent policy training, supporting Evolve through experience reuse. We assemble our initial source pool mainly from open-source datasets and web-accessible corpora, including imagetext pairs and other visionlanguage corpora, general videos, egocentric human videos, real-robot recordings, and robot simulation data. Video provides the main source of physical experience, complemented by imagetext supervision, native state and action channels, and tactile observations. Together, these sources cover diverse scenes, objects, embodiments, and manipulation tasks. The knowledge available in source can exceed the supervision made explicit by its original annotations. video may record objects, spatial relationships, intermediate goals, and state changes while its caption names only the overall activity. Relevant evidence may also occupy only brief interval within longer recording. Each learning objective requires different view of this information. For example, the same video of putting cup into cabinet can support grounding question about the cup, an instruction-conditioned prediction of its placement, and an action-learning example when corresponding recorded or reconstructed trajectories are available. When synchronized tactile observations are available, the same interaction can also support prediction of contact and loading during grasping or placement. Constructing these views requires us to locate the event, identify its participants and task structure, and align the context and target at the appropriate granularity. frame may suffice for spatial question, whereas visual prediction requires coherent transition and action prediction additionally requires aligned motion supervision. We therefore make the relevant knowledge explicit in the form each objective needs, while retaining the context needed to interpret it. This lets one experience contribute to several learning tasks, with each example focusing on specific capability. Figure 2 summarizes Task-Oriented Knowledge Refinement in three stages: source acquisition, unified annotation, and task-specific data preparation. The unified annotation stage performs semantic interpretation once per sample to create shared record of hierarchical task labels, event boundaries, and scene and action descriptions. It preserves the original observations and available state, action, and tactile streams, together with spatial, contact, and quality information, without filtering samples. 4 Innata-0 Technical Report Figure 2: Task-oriented knowledge refinement. Heterogeneous sources undergo unified annotation without sample filtering. Task-specific pipelines reuse the shared annotations to prepare supervision for visionlanguage understanding, video generation, policy training, and tactile generation, applying their own quality criteria. source may support multiple tasks according to its available observations and annotations. The visionlanguage pipeline uses shared spatial and task annotations to select observations and construct instructiontarget pairs through task-specific rewriting, followed by validation and distribution balancing. Existing public QA is validated and reformatted without regeneration. The video-generation pipeline uses shared temporal annotations for clip construction, applies frameand clip-level quality criteria for each training stage, and assembles descriptive or instructional prompts from shared scene and action descriptions. The policy pipeline pairs native or reconstructed motion with shared instructions and task intervals, unifies action semantics, and uses task, outcome, and quality annotations for trajectory filtering and multi-view assembly. For eligible human videos, this includes hand reconstruction and camera-aware motion alignment. The tactile pipeline combines sensor observations with shared contact, coverage, and validity records, followed by sensor-to-MANO alignment, regional proxy construction, and temporal alignment with visual and motion streams. One source can thus yield multiple training forms, depending on its available observations and supervision. 2.2. Unified Information Extraction and Annotation We attach shared annotation record to each source, preserving its original timestamps, camera views, source metadata, native state and action channels, and tactile observations where available. The record combines source-level context with frame-level and interval-level annotations. We prompt Qwen3.8-Flash-Next [12] once per sample to produce the applicable semantic, relational, temporal, and perceptual-quality fields in single structured response. Specialized perception models add dense masks to this record, alongside source-provided depth and camera calibration. Thus, one VLM pass supplies broad description of the experience, while dedicated visual modules recover spatial measurements and available tactile observations provide contact evidence for downstream tasks. Spatial and Geometric Annotation. We combine specialized perception models with source-provided depth and camera calibration to obtain object localization and spatial information. 5 Innata-0 Technical Report Detection, segmentation, and tracking. We use Grounding DINO [13] for object detection and SAM 3.1 [14, 15] for instance segmentation and video tracking. VLMs provide additional object detection and localization for data requiring further annotation. We retain boxes, masks, prediction scores where available, and cross-frame object identities linked to the shared entity record. Depth and 3D structure. We use source-provided depth-camera measurements, together with available camera intrinsics and extrinsics, to obtain spatial inputs and supervision signals. Semantic and Temporal Annotation. The shared VLM response describes scenes, interactions, and task structure through the following groups. Scene and entity context. We annotate scene categories, activity settings, workspace types, and viewpoint tags, including egocentric, external, and robot-mounted views. Entity records identify participating humans or robots, relevant objects and tools, observable object attributes, and their initial states. Scene tags describe the environment at multiple levels, such as an indoor setting, kitchen, and countertop workspace. We retain both categorical tags and concise natural-language descriptions. Object relations and interaction states. The shared VLM response explicitly annotates objectobject and actorobject relationships, complementing localized entities with language-grounded spatial descriptions [16]. These include directional relations such as left/right, above/below, and in front of/behind; topological relations such as inside, on, and supported by; and visible interaction states such as approaching, holding, touching, or releasing. Each relation identifies its participants and the frame or interval in which it holds. We also record changes in these relations, such as an object moving from supporting surface into container, and retain the viewpoint or coordinate context of each spatial description. Hierarchical tasks and verifiable subgoals. We annotate activity families, overall tasks, subtasks, and atomic goals at the granularity supported by each recording. Each subtask identifies the acting entity, relevant objects, and intended state change, together with concise instruction and an observable condition for judging completion. Links to the parent task and temporal ordering preserve its role in the overall activity. These annotations provide explicit, actor-centered units for execution and progress assessment. Temporal boundaries and execution stages. We annotate the start and end of tasks, subtasks, and atomic intervals, together with their ordering and execution stages. For selected robot demonstrations and egocentric recordings, the shared pass groups movements that serve one manipulation goal and marks new interval when that goal changes. Stage labels describe preparation, approach, interaction, and completion or termination where these phases are visible. We also identify pauses, repeated attempts, and transitions between goals, and associate observed state changes with the corresponding intervals. Action types and motion characteristics. We assign action-type labels such as reaching, grasping, lifting, transporting, placing, pushing, pulling, rotating, inserting, opening, closing, pouring, and releasing. Task labels describe the intended goal; action labels describe the motion or interaction used to pursue it. For each interval, we annotate the active hand or end effector, single-arm or bimanual execution, motion direction, and apparent motion magnitude. Magnitude tags describe qualitative amplitude, such as small, moderate, or large motion, separately for the manipulator and the manipulated object. We distinguish these visual assessments from metric displacement or joint-motion measurements available in native trajectories, and describe camera or viewpoint motion separately. Task outcomes, failures, and recovery. We annotate task and subtask outcomes with the visible state changes supporting them, recording partial completion or an undetermined result when the footage is incomplete. For recovery events, we link the preceding unsuccessful attempt to its corrective interval and describe the corrective behavior, such as regrasping slipped object, realigning an insertion, or retrying an opening motion. We record whether the correction restores the state needed to continue the original task and, where visible, identify the subtask pursued afterward. The outcomes of the initial attempt, recovery, and subsequent execution remain distinct. Native success flags are retained alongside 6 Innata-0 Technical Report video-based assessments. Static and Dynamic Description Cards. We organize the scene and action descriptions from the same structured response into static and dynamic cards. When recording stays in one setting, its clips share static card describing the workspace, lighting, and objects that remain in place; when the setting varies, we retain scene description for each clip. Each clip has dynamic card containing brief action summary and detailed description of its participants, movement, and state changes. For continuous actions, the description follows the movement; for discrete changes, it records the initial state, action, and visible outcome. In egocentric footage, we distinguish viewpoint changes from hand and object motion. The dynamic card also includes an instruction when manipulation is visible. Figure A.1 in the appendix shows how three clips from one recording share static card while retaining distinct action descriptions. Visual Quality, Visibility, and Temporal Integrity. We retain technical attributes and perceptual assessments in separate groups. Recording attributes. We extract resolution, aspect ratio, frame rate, duration, codec, and bitrate from source metadata. We retain the correspondence between derived clips and original frame timestamps. Perceptual quality and temporal continuity. The shared VLM response assesses defocus and motion blur, exposure, lighting, compression artifacts, camera shake, and jitter. It also identifies shot changes, apparent freezes or interruptions, abrupt viewpoint changes, and discontinuities in the visible action. We associate localized quality issues with their affected intervals. Embodiment and object visibility. We explicitly annotate whether the robot or human body, arms, hands or grippers, manipulated objects, and interaction regions remain visible. The record distinguishes partial cropping, complete departure from the frame, and occlusion by another entity, with entry or exit intervals where observable. We track body visibility separately from the visibility of the active manipulator and target object: robot base outside the frame can coexist with fully visible manipulation. These fields capture whether the evidence required for understanding an action or reconstructing its motion is present. Tactile Observations and Contact Evidence. Tactile observations provide local contact and force information for understanding physical interactions. The reliability of these observations, however, depends on signal quality and sensing coverage, which vary across sensing technologies and sensor configurations [17, 18]. We therefore apply source-specific baseline correction and denoising to suppress spurious responses caused by sensor noise and baseline drift. For complex sensor layouts with incomplete coverage, we record coverage and measurement validity separately from contact labels, so that missing or unreliable readings are not treated as evidence of no contact. The shared record retains these observations and annotations together with their source timestamps and correspondence to visual and motion streams. We populate fields according to the source modalities: images provide scene and spatial annotations, videos additionally provide temporal and motion evidence, and robotics records can supply native state and action channels, tactile observations, calibration, and outcome information. Each preparation branch applies its own quality requirements to these attributes. From Shared Annotations to Focused Supervision. The resulting annotations support non-exclusive routing into four preparation branches. The VLM branch constructs task-specific questions and targets from entity locations, spatial relations, task hierarchies, execution stages, and outcomes. The video-generation branch prepares captioned sequences using shared scene context, interval-level action descriptions, and stage-dependent quality filtering. The action branch combines the relevant intervals and instructions with native trajectories or reconstructed motion, then performs alignment, retargeting, trajectory filtering, and multi-view assembly as required. The tactile branch combines tactile observations with contact annotations and validity information to construct aligned tactile targets in common representation. source may contribute to several branches, with each selecting the observations, annotations, and supervision appropriate 7 Innata-0 Technical Report Figure 3: The embodied understanding data pipeline. Shared public sources and source-level annotations support task-conditioned screening, observationtarget construction, and quality control. Existing public QA follows separate validation and format-conversion path. The resulting corpus combines constructed task-focused supervision, public embodied data, and general multimodal data. to its learning objective. 2.3. Data for Embodied VisionLanguage Understanding The VLM branch converts the shared source annotations into task-focused supervision for embodied perception and reasoning. As illustrated in Figure 3, it selects task-compatible observations, constructs questions and targets grounded in the available evidence, and combines the resulting examples with public multimodal training corpora. Task Coverage and Specification. We organize supervision around object grounding, spatial reasoning, and temporal task understanding, including subtask identification and execution-stage recognition. Temporal segmentation and future-event or state prediction are included when sufficient evidence is available. Each task defines its observation requirements, relevant entities or events, and target format (e.g., text, discrete choices, spatial coordinates, or temporal intervals), guiding source selection and annotation. Task-Conditioned Source Selection. We draw from general videos, egocentric human videos, real-robot recordings, simulation data, and public visionlanguage corpora. Shared spatial, semantic, temporal, and quality annotations support task-conditioned screening for observable entities, interactions, and sufficient context. Selection criteria vary by task: clip unsuitable for precise localization may still support semantic recognition, while one source may serve multiple tasks. Observation and Supervision Construction. For each selected sourcetask pair, we assemble an image, multi-view image set, or video segment and construct an instructiontarget pair. Supervision comes directly from reliable annotations or through task-specific rewriting and model-assisted labeling. We preserve observationannotation correspondence and standardize target formats and coordinate conventions. For future prediction, targets may derive from subsequent observations, but model inputs exclude the future information being predicted. 8 Innata-0 Technical Report Quality Assurance and Distribution Control. We verify media availability, instructiontarget consistency, annotation support, and task-specific formatting, while retaining source provenance for deduplication and benchmark-overlap audits. To reduce distributional shortcuts, we inspect task coverage and answer distributions, downsample overrepresented binary or directional answers, and rebalance eligible multiplechoice options while preserving their semantics and grounding. These measures complement annotation validity checks. Integration with Public Multimodal Corpora. Constructed examples are combined with public embodied datasets and general-purpose multimodal corpora. Existing questionanswer data enter through validation and format conversion without regeneration. Public corpora provide broad visual and semantic coverage, while task-focused examples strengthen embodied supervision. Data Sources and Coverage. We assemble heterogeneous corpus covering general multimodal understanding, spatial perception, multi-view and video reasoning, language-conditioned grounding, affordance understanding, and robot-centric question answering. General-purpose data from Cambrian and LLaVAOneVision provide broad visual and instruction-following supervision. Embodied data supply complementary supervision for spatial relations, metric estimation, viewpoint changes, object localization, and interactionrelevant regions. Table B.1 in Appendix summarizes the public datasets and our task-focused constructed collection represented in the understanding-tower training mixtures. 2.4. Data for Video Generation The video-generation branch builds the visual dynamics foundation of the WAM from general videos, egocentric human videos, and robot videos. It prepares temporally coherent training sequences, generates captions matched to their content and temporal extent, and applies quality criteria appropriate to each training stage. General videos provide broad visual and motion coverage, while human and robot interaction videos focus learning on embodied events. Clip construction. We screen recordings before decoding, checking duration, frame dimensions, and frame rate against criteria suited to each data source. We extract each selected interval once from its designated camera view and store the clip in common video encoding. Quality scoring, captioning, and latent encoding then read the same clip file, reducing the need for format-specific preprocessing. Frameand clip-level scoring. On sampled frames, we measure brightness, saturation, and sharpness with classical image processing methods on the CPU. Brightness and saturation help flag poor exposure or loss of color. Gamma [19] rates perceptual quality, the LAION aesthetic predictor [20] scores visual appeal, and PaddleOCR [21, 22] locates text. We average LAION scores over the sampled frames of each clip. For OCR, we compare text locations across frames to flag fixed corner overlays. Persistence alone does not disqualify clip: product label may stay visible throughout an action. Models that score clip as whole include DOVER [23] for technical and aesthetic quality and VTSS [24] for suitability for video training. We retain each score with its clip and use stricter quality criteria to select the quality-tuning subset from the continued-pretraining pool. Prompt assembly. In each epoch of continued pretraining, we sample one prompt template compatible with each clips annotation fields. Descriptive prompts pair the scene with the observed action; instructions can appear with or without the scene. The same clip can thus be paired with description in one epoch and an instruction in another, as illustrated in Figure A.2. 2.5. Data for Action Generation The policy data pipeline prepares paired visual and motion supervision for Innata-0-WAM from public real-robot and simulation trajectories, together with motion reconstructed and retargeted from eligible 9 Innata-0 Technical Report human videos. Shared task and temporal annotations associate each trajectory segment with its execution objective. For caption variants that represent task progress, we pair the complete instruction with the active subtask and previously completed tasks, matching the task context supplied by the agent under the co-design protocol. Preparation unifies action semantics, refines trajectory quality, and assembles synchronized camera views. Trajectories collected during system rollouts follow the same annotation and preparation procedures. Successful execution segments, including corrective actions and post-recovery continuations, are retained for subsequent policy training, allowing validated system experience to contribute supervision through the shared pipeline. 2.5.1. Gripper Manipulation Data Gripper demonstrations span robot embodiments, tools, and control interfaces, so identical vector shapes can encode different physical quantities. pose may describe the wrist flange or grasp center, and an action field may contain controller command or subsequent measured state. We unify supervision around its physical meaning, enabling demonstrations from different embodiments to provide compatible learning targets while retaining their kinematic differences. Preparation therefore proceeds in two stages: semantic unification followed by trajectory quality filtering. The first establishes what each channel represents and when it applies; the second evaluates the reliability of the resulting trajectories. Stage 1: Unifying Action Semantics. For each embodiment, we first determine what each field in the source data means and then match each observation to its action target. These pairs form the basis for two representations of robot motion: one in predefined unified end-effector (EEF) space and the other in joint space. Canonical end-effector geometry and motion. We define fixed tool center point (TCP) at the center of the effective finger-pad grasp region in the closed reference configuration. Its +Z axis points from the palm toward the fingertips, +X follows the opening direction toward specified finger, and +Y completes right-handed frame. Matched tool and mounting transforms map source poses to this TCP; forward kinematics provides poses when measured joints are available but direct poses are unsuitable. Canonical geometry without historical calibration defines an explicitly identified virtual TCP. EEF State records the current TCP pose in declared reference frame, such as camera frame or robot base/body frame [25]. Both arms of bimanual embodiment share reference. We derive the pose component of EEF Action from consecutive measured states, expressing the current-to-next TCP transform in the current TCP frame. We order joints by name within each embodiment, using radians for revolute positions and meters for prismatic positions. For ordinary joint-position channels, State contains current measured positions and Action contains the next measured absolute positions, independently of the native controller interface. Available head, torso, and other joints remain represented, while mobile-base channels retain their declared pose or displacement semantics. Gripper opening and control signals. We normalize observed gripper opening to scale from 0 (fully closed) to 1 (fully open), using the limits specified in the URDF or manufacturer documentation. Some sources provide separate observation and control signals, with commands sometimes encoded as discrete values such as {1, 0, 1}. We prioritize observed gripper states during pretraining, then use control signals during supervised fine-tuning to match the target robots control interface. Layouts and storage. Joint uses fixed 128-channel layout covering arms, grippers, hands, head, torso, mobile base, legs, and extensions. EEF uses separate 20-channel layout, with ten channels per arm. Single-arm data only use the first ten. Unavailable channels are zero-filled and masked, with independent State and Action validity masks. LeRobot v3 episodes [28] retain source timestamps, row mappings, per-view video offsets, and task references. Explicit timestamp mappings establish observationtarget alignment; normalization remains separate from semantic unification. Original values, transformation metadata, proxies, and assumptions remain traceable. Stage 2: Trajectory Quality Filtering. We validate the standardized trajectories for non-finite active values, missing observations, invalid masks or rotations, and inconsistent episode or media boundaries. Motion diagnostics examine displacement, angular change, velocity, acceleration, jerk, local trend residuals, and oscillation where the timebase and reference frames support them. Thresholds depend on embodiment, representation, field, and sampling regime. Commandstate checks use only independent, semantically comparable commands; state-derived targets cannot independently validate their source states. We combine these diagnostics with shared task, subtask, outcome, and visual-quality annotations to reject defective trajectories or intervals. Trajectory validity is assessed separately from task outcome: successful corrective segments remain eligible even when earlier attempts failed, with their links to the failed attempt and subsequent task continuation preserved. When source outcome labels are reliable, they take precedence over model assessments. Low motion or high jerk alone does not establish corruption: task context distinguishes redundant idling from informative holding, contact, recovery, and waiting. Removing an interval splits trajectory into continuous episodes. We synchronize cuts across camera views and paired Joint/EEF representations, retain complete subtask descriptions with adjusted timestamps, and recompute or invalidate derived targets at boundaries. Targets never cross resets or removed gaps; terminal observations can remain without valid next-step targets. Paired representations count as one physical demonstration. Selective smoothing applies only to validated noise candidates. It operates on continuous position or joint sequences and treats rotations in rotation space, protecting contact events, gripper transitions, and task boundaries. We recompute observation-derived targets, preserve native commands, and retain correction only if consistency and event-preservation checks pass. 2.5.2. Dexterous Manipulation Data Dexterous demonstrations capture coordinated finger articulation for grasp adaptation and in-hand manipulation, extending the opening-and-closing supervision provided by gripper data. Differences in hand mechanisms, joint encodings, and EEF frames make this supervision difficult to combine across embodiments. We inherit the two-stage pipeline described for gripper data in Section 2.5.1, reusing its visual processing, semantic annotations, and general trajectory checks. Here we detail the adaptations needed to align articulated hands and their motion. Table C.6 in Appendix C.2.3 lists the action-learning sources, including complementary instrumented and robot demonstrations. 11 Innata-0 Technical Report Unified hand representation. Robot hands differ in joint counts, axes, and link arrangements, so their native coordinates do not provide common articulation standard. Despite these structural differences, hands exploit common object affordances to accomplish similar goals, such as grasping handle or turning lid. These shared interactions motivate aligning hand motion by its functional role, allowing demonstrations from different embodiments to be related to common task semantics and contact evidence. We therefore design Hand32 around human-hand anatomy, following the functional alignment principle of FAAS [29]. Each coordinate identifies finger, joint level, and motion function: flexion, abduction, or twist. The thumb contributes seven angular coordinates and each other finger six, yielding 31 shared coordinates and one reserved for declared embodiment-specific extension. Robot and human demonstrations thus share an articulation interface while retaining the motions supported by each hand. Mapping diverse hand mechanisms. The human-hand reference does not imply one-to-one joint correspondence: mechanical joints can occupy different locations, several axes can realize one finger function, and single motor can drive several joints. Mapping therefore accounts for both the intended motion and the mechanism that produces it. We first identify corresponding finger functions from the source kinematic chain and reconcile joint axes, neutral positions, and units. Where direct correspondence is insufficient, inverse kinematics matches aligned finger endpoints to support mappings between multiple source and reference degrees of freedom. Threeor four-finger hands use explicit functional finger correspondences, with missing digits and motions masked. Known mimic relations remain coupling constraints, while whole-finger drive values use declared equivalent-angle conversions. Task Structure and Execution To support Plan, Innata-0-Agent coordinates model execution across interdependent subtasks to accomplish long-horizon tasks. Given user instruction, the agent organizes the task based on the models execution capabilities and retrieves relevant hierarchical memory to construct the current task context and WAM command. WAM then executes the assigned subtask through action chunks in the robot or simulator. During execution, the agent periodically reviews task progress and updates the active subtask and WAM command based on observed outcomes. This forms closed loop of task planning, physical execution, and progress-driven adaptation. 4.1.1. Hierarchical Memory Architecture Long-horizon interaction requires the system to maintain an evolving task state rather than repeatedly reasoning from the original instruction [64]. We therefore introduce hierarchical memory architecture that progressively organizes physical interaction evidence into task-relevant state and reusable knowledge. Together, these memories provide shared state substrate for task decomposition, planning, verification, recovery, and model execution. Task Memory. During execution, the agent continuously compresses the interaction history into taskcentric state that summarizes current progress, completed subtasks, unresolved dependencies, relevant object states, detected anomalies, and recovery outcomes. This evolving summary provides the primary context for long-horizon reasoning, avoiding the need to reconstruct the task state repeatedly from the full execution history. At fixed intervals, the agent reviews the current task stage using the latest observations and execution evidence, and updates the task memory accordingly. Physical State Memory. Physical state memory maintains shared account of the evolving physical world through complementary spatial and tactile components. The spatial component maintains persistent object locations, scene structure, and spatial relations beyond the current field of view. It provides stable grounding for task-state tracking and allows planning and recovery to reason about objects or regions that are temporarily occluded or no longer directly observed [65, 66]. The tactile component contributes sparse but interactionrich evidence about local contact, particularly when interactions are visually ambiguous [67, 68]. The agent interprets this feedback together with visual and proprioceptive observations to retain verified interaction states, such as whether an object remains held or has been released. Together, the two components ground the task state in both the spatial arrangement of the scene and ongoing physical interactions. Causal Interaction Memory. At the highest abstraction level, validated interaction experience is consolidated into reusable knowledge about how actions transform physical states. Causal memory represents actioncentered preconditions and effects over structured object states and relations [69]: Precondition Action Effect. (11) This abstraction allows experience obtained from previous interactions to be grounded to the current state and reused for action selection, forward prediction, backward reasoning, and recovery without requiring 29 Innata-0 Technical Report immediate model updates. The memory hierarchy therefore supports bidirectional information flow. During execution, spatial and tactile evidence updates the agent-summarized task state, while validated state transitions are progressively consolidated into causal knowledge. During decision making, relevant causal experience is grounded back into the current task and physical state to guide planning, execution, and recovery. 4.1.2. Grounded Perception and Execution Building on hierarchical memory, the agent decomposes long-horizon objective into causally ordered subtasks and dispatches them to WAM for grounded execution. We further introduce periodic stagereview mechanism to automatically govern when the active subtask should be maintained or advanced. At each review, the agent samples earlier keyframes and recent observations to analyze the visible state transition after the robot or simulator executes an action chunk produced by WAM. This temporal evidence is interpreted together with the within-episode task memory, available spatial and tactile memory, and the subtask dependencies and temporal knowledge retrieved from long-term hierarchical memory. The reviewer then determines whether the expected physical effect of the current subtask is visually supported, classifying its status as completed, in progress, or uncertain. subtask transition is accepted only when completion is supported by sufficient evidence; the completed stage is then added to the task history, and the next subtask and corresponding WAM command are activated. Otherwise, WAM continues executing the current command while subsequent reviews accumulate additional evidence. This process couples high-level task progression with grounded execution without requiring WAM itself to infer the global task structure or decide when to switch subtasks. Every review is recorded, including the environment step, the stage index before and after the review, whether the transition was accepted, and the complete structured decision returned by the model. These records make the evolution of the task structure auditable and provide reusable execution evidence for subsequent analysis and system improvement. The overall execution process therefore alternates between WAM action generation and conservative, evidence-grounded stage review, enabling long-horizon tasks to progress without relying on privileged simulator state or allowing the model to advance the plan from unsupported assumptions. 4.2. Verification and Adaptive Recovery To support Recover, Innata-0-Agent handles uncertainties and unexpected failures during real-world execution through physical outcome verification and adaptive recovery. Physical actions may produce unintended outcomes due to partial observability, contact uncertainty, or changes in the environment. To address these challenges, the agent continuously monitors execution progress through environmental feedback and verifies whether the intended physical outcomes have been achieved [70, 71]. When deviations occur, the agent analyzes their causes and selects appropriate recovery strategies [71, 72]. It then invokes complementary embodied tools and skills to restore valid execution conditions. Depending on the recovery outcome, subsequent execution proceeds through either WAM or agent-controlled tools to complete the remaining task. This closed-loop process connects physical outcome verification with adaptive recovery, allowing the system to sustain task progress under uncertainty. 4.2.1. Execution Monitoring and Intervention During nominal execution, WAM repeatedly predicts and executes action chunks, while the agent evaluates task progress at scheduled verification checkpoints. Each verification constructs compact temporal evidence bundle from sampled historical keyframes and recent observations, allowing the agent to compare the observed state transition with the physical effect expected under the current task context. The resulting decision describes whether an anomaly should be triggered, the corresponding failure type, the supporting 30 Innata-0 Technical Report evidence, and the discrepancy between the observed and expected physical changes. Slow progress or visual ambiguity alone is not treated as failure; intervention is initiated only when positive temporal evidence indicates that execution has deviated from the intended task progression. In addition to periodic verification, the system adaptively increases the review frequency around potentially high-risk interactions, such as changes in gripper state during grasping or object transport. This event-driven scheduling concentrates reasoning on contact-sensitive phases without continuously querying the reasoning model. Temporal cooldowns suppress repeated triggers caused by the same persistent visual symptom, preventing redundant interventions. Once an anomaly has been verified, WAM execution is suspended and control is transferred to the agent. This handoff occurs directly in the current live environment. The agent inherits the same scene instance, object configuration, robot joint and gripper states, environment step, and remaining execution budget. 4.2.2. Tool-based Verification and Recovery To support recovery across different tasks and anomaly modes, we collect general and extensible tool set. Rather than directly generating low-level control code, the recovery agent selects tools, instantiates their bounded parameters, and composes them into short closed-loop intervention sequences. The tool set is organized into four functional layers. Observation tools expose task information, robot state, synchronized visual observations, camera calibration, and previously discovered scene entities without changing the environment. Perception tools convert these observations into actionable semantic and geometric representations, including target segmentation, three-dimensional measurement, and transformations between image and world coordinates. Motion adaptation tools provide parameterized geometric adjustments that allow the agent to retarget the end-effector, execute contact-aware arc motions, or reposition the mobile base according to the current scene. Finally, atomic skills encapsulate bounded and repeatedly physical operations, such as actuating the gripper, returning the arm to safe configuration, maintaining pose, or performing geometry-conditioned rim grasp. These layers support different stages of the closed-loop workflow. During verification, the agent primarily uses observation and perception tools to inspect the evolving scene, ground task-relevant entities, and determine whether the intended physical effect has occurred. Utilizing these tools, the agent can gather additional evidence and reduce semantic or geometric uncertainty. Their outputs supplement the temporal evidence used to distinguish normal progress, ambiguous observations, and verified anomalies. Once an anomaly has been verified, the same observation and perception interface provides the grounded diagnosis and geometric targets required for recovery. The agent can then introduce motion-adaptation tools and atomic skills to modify the live physical state. Candidate motions may first be checked for feasibility before bounded physical primitive is executed through the native robot or simulator interface. Verification and recovery therefore share consistent representation of objects, geometry, and robot state, avoiding separate perception pipeline at the point of intervention. Tool use follows an iterative observereasonactverify process. The agent acquires evidence, selects tool according to the current task or diagnosed failure, executes the tool, and incorporates its result into the next decision. Fresh observations are collected after physical intervention to determine whether the intended local change has occurred. Unsuccessful actions, geometric constraints, and tool-level failure feedback are retained in the interaction history, enabling the agent to revise parameters, select different tool, or terminate an ineffective strategy rather than repeatedly issuing the same intervention. 4.3. It reaches 50.0% on Insert HDMI and 99.0% on Lift Bottle, demonstrating its ability to handle both precise insertion and stable grasp maintenance. These results suggest that the learned tactile representation retains contact 42 Innata-0 Technical Report information useful for different forms of manipulation. On Bench2Dex  (Table 11)  , the same pretrained WAM achieves an overall score of 53.82 within the agent system, outperforming all the compared methods on the selected ten-task subset. It ranks first on Baking Tray Prep (T32), Breadbasket Fast-Food Loading (T60), and Sports Ball Cup Sort (T64), with scores of 51.76, 72.79, and 58.45, respectively. Performance across these two benchmarks suggests that the shared regional representation provides useful foundation for learning contact-rich control across different sensors and embodiments. By bringing heterogeneous tactile data into common format, tactile mid-training allows task-specific fine-tuning to build on interaction experience collected from multiple sources. Long-horizon tasks further illustrate the benefits of our model-agent co-design. Fridge Wine Interhand Pour (T34) involves complex bimanual handovers that are difficult for existing coding agents to execute, while Bimanual Piano Playing (T79) places demanding sequencing and timing requirements on standalone WAM/VLA policies. The co-designed system achieves competitive results on both. The agent maintains the task structure and updates the current subgoal, while the WAM generates the dexterous motions needed to carry it out. These results support our co-design of task-level orchestration and learned manipulation, combining their strengths to address tasks that challenge either component alone. 6. Limitations and Future Directions While Innata-0 has demonstrated promising progress in embodied understanding, world prediction, and robotic manipulation, challenges remain toward native embodied intelligence. Generalization across environments, tasks, and robot embodiments warrants further exploration. More extensive real-world validation is needed to assess system generalization across robot embodiments, diverse environments, and increasingly complex tasks, as well as robustness to dynamic changes and unexpected failures during physical interaction. Looking ahead, we see opportunities to advance both model and agent capabilities. On the model side, we aim to improve generalization across tasks and robot embodiments, strengthen physical understanding and prediction, and support more complex dexterous manipulation. This requires expanding the diversity, quality, and coverage of embodied data, including egocentric videos, real-robot trajectories, tactile interactions, and dexterous manipulation data. We also aim to leverage real-world execution and recovery experiences for iterative model improvement and continual agent evolution toward more generalizable and reliable native embodied world systems. On the agent side, we aim to advance multimodal reasoning with richer visual, spatial, and tactile information. We also plan to explore in-context learning and experience retrieval to improve adaptation to unfamiliar situations. Reducing token consumption and optimizing inference efficiency will also be important for scalable, real-world deployment. 7. Unified Annotation Records These examples illustrate the shared annotation layer in Section 2.2. One reusable record combines scene descriptions, task goals, temporal intervals, execution outcomes, and quality attributes; captions are one downstream use. It retains links to the original task text, native trajectory channels, and sensor timestamps. Fields are populated only with source support: video may support semantic event boundaries without providing metric joint motion or tactile measurements. A.1. Shared Context and Interval-Level Descriptions One scene, three actions. The three clips in Figure A.1 share scene context and task-level annotations. Dynamic cards describe separating the broom and dustpan, sweeping paper into the dustpan, and emptying it into bin. The sweeping description follows repeated broom strokes; the emptying description captures state change: the left arm tips the dustpan containing crumpled paper and blue wrapper over the bin, then lowers it empty. Consistent references to the left and right grippers, tools, paper, and bin connect descriptions, task intervals, and visible relations, such as paper resting in the dustpan before being deposited in the bin. Understanding Training Details We adapt the understanding tower through staged supervised training pipeline that combines broad spatial and embodied learning with task-focused refinement. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B [16], the training progressively emphasizes spatial understanding while retaining general-purpose visual supervision. Below, we describe the data composition and training trajectory of the evaluated checkpoint, distinguishing the available source inventory, the prepared training mixtures, and the supervised sample exposures actually consumed. For mid-training, our source inventory contains approximately 63.6M candidate records, of which 60.8M are eligible after source-specific preprocessing and validation. The eligible inventory comprises approximately 11.7M general-purpose records and 49.2M embodied-oriented records, including internally assembled collections. These figures describe source-pool records rather than globally deduplicated examples or actual training exposure. From this inventory, we prepare 20M-example mid-training mixture, with approximately 13.3% general-purpose and 86.7% embodied-oriented data by source category. Detailed datasets are shown in Table B.1. Training proceeds from broad mid-training to task-focused post-training. Mid-training emphasizes large spatial and embodied datasets while retaining general-purpose supervision. Post-training first applies task-balanced multi-source mixture and then refines the model with the curated questionanswer collection, compact task-specific training sets, and general-purpose replay. The final refinement mixture contains 57,565 task-focused examples, 42,737 examples from compact task-specific sets, and 20,000 generalpurpose examples. The compact sets comprise EmbSpatial-SFT, MindCube, and the ERQA-related training subsets of Embodied-R1.5. We fine-tune both the language and visual components using AdamW with 𝛽1 = 0.9, 𝛽2 = 0.95, 𝜖 = 108, and weight decay of 0.1. Training uses bfloat16 computation, fully sharded data parallelism, activation checkpointing, and gradient-norm clipping at 1.0. Implementation of the Embodied Tool Set We implement general and extensible embodied tool set shared by verification and recovery. The tools are organized into four functional groups according to their role in closed-loop interaction: Observation, Perception, Motion adjustment and Atomic skills. Observation and perception tools do not advance the environment, whereas motion-adjustment tools and atomic skills act through the native robot or simulator interface and consume simulation steps. The full tool set is displayed in Table F.1. Figure F.1: Per-task recovery gains on the 32 RoboCasa365 composite tasks. Each stacked bar reports the success rate of Innata-0. Dark blue denotes episodes completed natively by the Innata-0-WAM, while light blue denotes additional successes obtained through online recovery. Tasks are grouped into the Composite-Seen and Composite-Unseen splits. Percentages above the bars indicate the final success rate after recovery, and values inside the light-blue segments indicate the absolute percentage-point improvement contributed by recovery. F.2. Detailed Result Analysis Per-task recovery analysis. Figure F.1 shows that the benefits of recovery are strongly task-dependent and concentrate on those challenging tasks for native Innata-0-WAM. In the Composite-Seen split, recovery provides substantial gains on tasks such as SearingMeat and SetUpCuttingStation. The improvements are even more pronounced on several Composite-Unseen tasks, including BreadSelection, CategorizeCondiments, PanTransfer, RecycleBottlesByType, and WashFruitColander. In contrast, tasks with already strong native performance, such as PreSoakPan, ScrubCuttingBoard, and GarnishPancake, require little or no recovery intervention. These results suggest that recovery primarily compensates for WAM failures under difficult or unfamiliar conditions, rather than uniformly altering otherwise successful executions. 86 Innata-0 Technical Report Table F.1: Embodied tool set.
